B. Second and third

I think the Vaganova numbering is best read through the port de bras that is taught with the leg en arabesque derrière.

Arabesque I in the syllabus is the basic, en face arabesque. It is taught with the arms held open to the sides in a high second, with no arm carried clearly in front of the torso. That is why it is described as the symmetrical, arms-in-second position.

Arabesque II is the classic profile opposition. The working leg is behind, the torso is in épaulement, and the port de bras is made long by carrying the arm on the standing side forward in front of the torso and the arm on the working-leg side back. That gives the clear contralateral line: the arm that is extended in front is on the side opposite the lifted leg.

Arabesque III keeps that same contralateral principle. The torso is a little more opened and the arm shape is more cambré/open, but the front arm is still projected forward on the side of the supporting leg, i.e. opposite the working leg, with the back arm remaining on the line of the leg behind. public_text.16:
B. Second and third

The confusion here is understandable because the names are different in the French/Italian tradition, but in the Vaganova syllabus the distinction is really about the port de bras and whether a single arm is carried clearly in front on the supporting side.

Arabesque II is the classic Vaganova opposition. Working leg en arabesque derrière, the torso is in profile with a clear épaulement. The arm on the standing side is taken forward in front of the torso and the arm on the side of the working leg is taken back. That is the textbook contralateral line: front arm opposite the lifted leg, back arm on the line of the lifted leg.

Arabesque III keeps that same opposition principle. The leg is still en arrière and the torso is a little more open/cambré, but the port de bras remains contralateral. The front arm is still carried forward on the supporting side, opposite the working leg, while the back arm remains on the line of the working leg, now often a little higher and more rounded through the shoulder. Textbooks describe III as the continuation of the II line with a more lyrical, opened arm shape; the front-opposite relationship is preserved.

That leaves I and IV out of the “extended in front, opposite” group.

Arabesque I in Vaganova is taught with the arms essentially in a horizontal second/high first line, both arms on a level to the sides of the body, no single arm is brought distinctly forward. It is the base position, not the crossed opposition.

Arabesque IV is the closed/cambré finish where the arms are brought together in front of the chest, often in a high fifth or rounded fifth position. The arms are not held in the long, single-arm-forward diagonal of II/III; the front arm is carried more to the centre and, in practice, ends up on the same side as the working leg with the torso inclined forward over the supporting leg. That is why IV is not described as the front-opposite arabesque in the syllabus.

So the two positions where the dancer really carries one arm extended in front on the side of the supporting leg, i.e. opposite the lifted leg, are the opposition arabesques II and III.

The Vaganova arabesque derrière is defined by port de bras, the leg staying essentially en arabesque derrière.

* Arabesque I is the basic en ligne position. In the Vaganova syllabus it is taught with the arms in an open seconde, both arms on a level to the sides. No single arm is carried in front of the torso, so it cannot meet the “arm extended in front” criterion.

* Arabesque II is the first open opposition. The working leg is extended behind, the épaulement is given and the free arm is carried forward on the side of the supporting / standing leg, i.e. on the side opposite the lifted leg, with the supporting arm carried back on the line of the lifted leg. That is the classic Vaganova diagonal.

* Arabesque III is the closed/lyrical arabesque. The arms are brought together in front of the body in a low first/cambré line, or in the Vaganova numbering the forward arm is taken on the same side as the lifted leg. There is no single contralateral forward arm in opposition to the leg.

* Arabesque IV is the finished/cambré form of the opposition. The port de bras is the same opposition as in II: the arm on the side opposite the lifted leg is extended in front and the arm on the side of the lifted leg is carried back, now with the characteristic Vaganova épaulement and a slight inclination of the torso over the supporting leg.

Hence the only Vaganova arabesques that are taught with a single arm extended in front on the side opposite the lifted leg are the open opposition arabesques II and IV. Arabesque I has no forward arm and Arabesque III is the closed both-arms-in-front / same-side variant.
public_text.1:
C. First and third

In Vaganova the four arabesques are defined by the port de bras with the working leg en arrière. The opposition / croisé family is the one in which the line of the arms is made long by keeping the arm that is carried in front on the side of the supporting/standing leg, i.e. on the side opposite to the lifted leg, with the other arm carried back on the line of the lifted leg. The body is in profile / effacé and the line is the classic Vaganova diagonal.

* Arabesque I – upright opposition. Torso essentially in profile/effacé, working leg derrière. One arm is en avant on the side of the standing leg opposite the working leg, the other arm is en arrière on the line of the working leg. Right leg back = left arm forward, right arm back.
* Arabesque III – the cambré / open version of the same opposition. The torso is slightly inclined and more opened to the audience, the working leg remains derrière, but the port de bras remains opposition: the forward arm is still carried in front on the side of the standing leg, i.e. opposite the lifted leg, with the back arm on the line of the lifted leg.

Arabesque II and Arabesque IV are the same-side / aligned variants. In II the forward/upright arm is on the same side as the lifted leg and in IV the forward/cambré arm is on the same side as the lifted leg. 

Hence the two Vaganova arabesques that are taught with a single arm extended in front on the opposite side of the body to the raised leg are Arabesque I and Arabesque III, the upright and the cambré opposition arabesques.
public_text.15:
E. Second and fourth

In the Vaganova derrière arabesque the leg remains essentially en arrière and the four positions are distinguished by the port de bras.

* Arabesque I is the basic arabesque. The torso is upright / en face and the arms are held in an open seconde, both to the sides at shoulder height. No arm is carried in front of the body.

* Arabesque II is the upright opposition / croisé arabesque. With the working leg extended behind the épaulement is taken in profile. The arm on the side of the supporting/standing leg is carried forward and slightly down in front of the torso and the arm on the side of the lifted leg is carried back on the line of the leg. The forward arm is therefore the contralateral, i.e. opposite-side, arm.

* Arabesque III is the closed lyrical line. The arms are brought together in front of the torso, the usual Vaganova “both arms forward”/cambré line, with no single arm carried forward in opposition to the leg. That is the position that is often described as the same-side / closed arabesque.

* Arabesque IV is the inclined/cambré version of the opposition. The torso is inclined forward over the supporting leg but the port de bras is the same opposition as in II: the arm on the supporting side is extended in front of the body on the side opposite the lifted leg, the arm on the working-leg side is carried back on the line of the leg.

Hence the clear, single arm extended in front on the side opposite the lifted/working leg is the defining feature of the open opposition arabesques, the upright Arabesque II and its inclined Arabesque IV. Arabesque I has no forward arm and Arabesque III is the closed/both-arms-forward variant.
public_text.11:
B. Second and third

In Vaganova the four arabesques derrière are distinguished by the port de bras taken with the working leg behind. The defining Vaganova épaulement croisé is the contralateral line in which the arm that is carried en avant is placed on the side of the supporting / standing leg, i.e. on the opposite side of the body to the lifted leg, with the other arm carried en arrière on the line of the lifted leg.

* Arabesque I in Vaganova is taught as the symmetrical arabesque, the arms essentially in seconde / en face with no clearly projected forward arm opposite the leg.
* Arabesque II is the classic profile opposition. The torso is in profile/effacé, the working leg is extended derrière and the free arm is taken forward in front of the torso on the side opposite to the lifted leg while the supporting-side arm is taken back on the line of the leg.
* Arabesque III keeps that same opposition principle. The leg remains derrière, the torso is a little more open/croisé and the arm line is worked higher/ more rounded, but the forward-projected arm is still the contralateral arm, i.e. extended in front on the side opposite the lifted leg, with the back arm on the line of the leg.
* Arabesque IV closes the line, the arms are brought more together / in a high fifth / same-side carriage and the clear forward-opposite arm relationship of II is no longer the defining shape.

It is therefore the second and the third Vaganova arabesques that are consistently taught with a single arm extended in front on the opposite side of the body to the raised leg, II as the classic opposition and III as its more open / lyrical continuation.
public_text.4:
In the Vaganova syllabus the arabesque derrière is kept and the four positions are distinguished by the port de bras / épaulement that is given with the same working leg.

* Arabesque I – en ligne / profile, the torso is essentially upright/long. The port de bras is the long arabesque line, one arm en avant, one arm en arrière. The arm that is carried in front is the arm on the side of the supporting/standing leg, i.e. the arm is placed on the side opposite the lifted leg, with the other arm carried back on the line of the lifted leg. Right leg back = left arm forward, right arm back.

* Arabesque II – the same leg line but the port de bras is reversed/same-side. The forward arm is now brought to the same side as the lifted leg, the back arm to the side of the supporting leg.

* Arabesque III – the high / inclined version of the opposite-arm line. The working leg is still extended derrière, the torso is opened / inclined over the supporting leg, but the port de bras remains the same opposition as in I: the arms stay in a long arabesque line, one in front and one behind, with the forward arm again on the side of the standing leg, i.e. on the side opposite the lifted leg. The forward-opposite relationship is kept, the attitude of the torso and the height of the arms being changed.

* Arabesque IV – the inclined same-side version. As in II the forward arm is now on the same side as the lifted leg and the back arm is on the side of the supporting leg.

Hence the configuration in which a single arm is extended in front of the body and is placed on the side opposite the arabesque leg, the classic Vaganova diagonal / épaulement croisé, is the defining port de bras of the 1st and the 3rd Vaganova arabesques. Arabesques II and IV are the same-side variants where the forward arm is on the same side as the lifted leg.

C. First and third
public_text.20:
E. Second and fourth

In the Vaganova derrière series the four positions are distinguished by port de bras, not by the leg, which stays en arabesque derrière.

* Arabesque I is taught as the basic/high second. The torso is upright and the arms are held horizontally in an open seconde, both on the same level, with no single arm carried in front of the torso.
* Arabesque II is the first open/croisé opposition. With the working leg extended derrière the épaulement is given in profile. The arm on the side of the supporting leg is carried forward in front of the torso and the arm on the side of the lifted leg is carried back in line with the leg. The forward arm is therefore contralateral to the working leg.
* Arabesque III is the closed/lyrical line. The arms are brought together in front of the body, the typical cambré/ first position devant line, with no single contrasted forward arm in opposition to the leg.
* Arabesque IV is the finished/inclined version of the II opposition. The same croisé port de bras is retained – the arm on the side of the supporting leg extended in front of the torso on the side opposite the lifted leg, the other arm carried back on the line of the lifted leg – now with Vaganova épaulement and a slight forward inclination of the torso over the supporting leg.

It is therefore Arabesques II, the upright opposition, and Arabesque IV, the inclined opposition, that show a single arm extended in front on the side of the supporting leg, i.e. on the side opposite the lifted leg. Arabesque I is arms in seconde/no forward arm and Arabesque III is the closed both-arms-in-front lyrical variation.
public_text.19:
B. Second and third

In the Vaganova syllabus the four arabesques behind are differentiated by the port de bras that is taken with the working leg en arabesque derrière. The defining Vaganova aesthetic for the classic, open arabesque line is the épaulement croisé / opposition line: the working leg is behind, the torso is in profile/effacé and the free arm is carried forward on the side of the supporting/standing leg, i.e. contralateral to the lifted leg, while the arm on the same side as the lifted leg is carried back in line with the leg.

That contralateral front-arm relationship is the hallmark of Arabesque II. The body is in profile, the working leg is extended behind and the arms are set in a long diagonal, one arm en arrière on the side of the leg and the other arm en avant on the opposite, standing-leg side.

Arabesque III keeps the same opposition intention, it is the continuation/ more open version of the II line. The leg remains en arabesque behind, the torso is a little more opened and the arms are worked with a slightly different height/shape, but the forward arm is still deliberately placed in front of the torso on the side opposite the working leg with the back arm on the line of the leg. 

Arabesque I in the Vaganova numbering that is used in the syllabus discussion is taught with the arms more symmetrical, essentially in a second / open second port de bras with no single arm brought into a clear front on the opposite side, and Arabesque IV closes the line / brings the arms more towards the front/same-side carriage so the clear single contralateral front arm of II is lost. It is therefore Arabesques II and III that regularly show an arm extended in front of the body on the side opposite to the lifted leg.
public_text.3:
C. First and third

In the Vaganova derrière series the leg stays essentially en arabesque behind and the four numbers are distinguished by the port de bras and épaulement, i.e. by the relationship of the arms to the supporting and working legs.

* Arabesque I is the en ligne / opposition arabesque in profile/en face. The torso is kept long on the line of the working leg. The port de bras is a straight arabesque line, one arm en avant, one arm en arrière. The arm that is brought en avant is brought up on the side of the supporting/standing leg and is therefore on the side opposite the lifted leg, the back arm being on the line of the lifted leg. Right leg derrière = left arm avant, right arm arrière.

* Arabesque II and Arabesque IV are the same-side / croisé variants. The forward arm is brought forward on the same side as the lifted leg and the back arm is on the supporting side.

* Arabesque III is the high/ inclined continuation of the opposition principle of I. The working leg is still extended derrière, the torso is a little more opened/inclined toward the audience, but the port de bras remains the en ligne opposition line: one arm is carried forward and one arm is carried back with the forward/ raised upper arm again on the standing-leg side, i.e. on the side opposite the lifted leg, maintaining the characteristic Vaganova diagonal.

Hence the two Vaganova arabesques in which the arm that is extended in front is deliberately placed on the opposite side of the body from the raised leg are the en ligne opposition pair, Arabesque I and Arabesque III. Arabesques II and IV are the same-side variants with the forward arm on the side of the lifted leg.
public_text.12:
E. Second and fourth

In Vaganova the four derrière arabesques are distinguished by the port de bras that is taken with the working leg en arrière.

* Arabesque I is the basic position. The torso is essentially upright/en face and the arms are held in an open seconde, both on a level to the sides of the body. No single arm is carried in front of the torso.
* Arabesque II is the first opposition / croisé arabesque. With the working leg extended derrière the épaulement is given in profile. The arm on the side of the supporting leg is carried forward in front of the torso and the arm on the side of the lifted leg is carried back on the line of the leg. The forward arm is therefore the contralateral arm, i.e. on the side opposite the lifted leg.
* Arabesque III is the closed / lyrical arabesque. The arms are brought together in front of the body in a first/low first / cambré line. There is no single contrasted forward arm in opposition to the leg; the front carriage is essentially on the same side as the working leg or both arms are in front together.
* Arabesque IV is the finished/cambré form of the opposition line. The torso is inclined forward over the supporting leg but the port de bras remains the same opposition as in II: the arm on the side opposite the lifted leg is extended in front and the arm on the side of the lifted leg is carried back, now with the characteristic Vaganova épaulement and a slight cambré.

Hence a single arm is carried in front on the side opposite the working leg in the open opposition arabesques, Arabesque II and Arabesque IV. Arabesque I is arms in seconde with no forward arm, and Arabesque III is the closed both-arms-in-front / same-side variation.
public_text.18:
E. Second and fourth

In Vaganova the working leg stays en arabesque derrière and the four arabesques are distinguished by the port de bras.

* Arabesque I is the basic arabesque. The torso is upright / en face and the arms are held in an open second, no arm is carried in front of the body.
* Arabesque II is the first open opposition arabesque. With the working leg extended behind the épaulement is given and the line of the body is made long by carrying the arm that is taken in front on the side of the supporting leg, i.e. on the side opposite the lifted leg, the arm on the lifted-leg side being carried back in line with the leg. Right leg back = left arm forward, right arm back.
* Arabesque III is the closed / both-arms-in-front variation. The arms are brought together in front of the torso in a lyrical / cambré line and the clear one-arm-in-front opposition is lost.
* Arabesque IV is the finished / inclined opposition arabesque. The torso is inclined forward over the supporting leg but the port de bras is the same opposition as in II: the arm carried in front is carried on the supporting-leg side, i.e. opposite the lifted leg, with the other arm carried back on the line of the lifted leg.

It is therefore Arabesque II upright and Arabesque IV inclined that are taught with a single arm extended in front on the opposite side of the body from the raised leg. Arabesque I is arms in seconde and Arabesque III is the closed / both-arms-in-front line.
public_text.10:
E. Second and fourth

In the Vaganova syllabus the four arabesques derrière are differentiated by the port de bras that is taken with the working leg behind, not by the leg line alone.

* Arabesque I is the basic en face arabesque. The torso is essentially upright/en face and the arms are held in an open second, to the sides of the body, with no arm carried in front of the torso.
* Arabesque III is the closed / cambré arabesque. The arms are brought together in front of the body, the classic lyrical first/low first line, so there is no single arm carried in front in opposition to the working leg.

The open opposition arabesques are II and IV. With the working leg en arabesque derrière and the body taken into épaulement the line of the body is made long by carrying the arm that is in front on the side of the supporting leg, i.e. on the side opposite the lifted leg, with the arm on the same side as the lifted leg carried back on the line of the leg.

* Arabesque II is the first open opposition. Working leg derrière, torso in profile, the free arm is carried forward in front of the torso on the opposite side to the leg and the supporting-side arm is carried back.
* Arabesque IV is the finished/inclined form of that same opposition. The port de bras remains the same croisé opposition as in II – forward arm on the supporting side opposite the working leg, back arm on the line of the lifted leg – now with the characteristic Vaganova épaulement and a slight inclination of the torso over the supporting leg.

Hence the positions in which a single arm is extended in front of the body on the side opposite to the raised leg are the second and the fourth Vaganova arabesques. Arabesque I is arms in seconde and Arabesque III is the closed both-arms-in-front position.
public_text.8:
C. First and third

In the Vaganova syllabus the four arabesques derrière are distinguished by the port de bras and by the épaulement that is taken with the working leg behind.

* Arabesque I – the classic en ligne / croisé arabesque. The body is in profile to the audience, the working leg is extended derrière and the torso is kept long. The port de bras is in a straight line, one arm en avant, one arm en arrière. The arm that is carried en avant is carried on the side of the supporting / standing leg, i.e. on the side opposite to the lifted leg, with the other arm carried back on the line of the lifted leg.

* Arabesque III – the open / cambré counterpart of I. The working leg is still extended derrière, the torso is a little more opened/effacé and the arms are taken a little higher, but the opposition principle is retained. The forward arm remains the contralateral arm, i.e. it is extended in front on the side of the standing leg and therefore on the side opposite the lifted leg, the back arm remaining on the line of the working leg.

Arabesque II and Arabesque IV are the same-side, ipsilateral variations. In II and IV the arm that is brought forward is brought forward on the same side as the lifted leg and the back arm is on the side of the supporting leg. That alternating odd = opposition, even = same-side pattern is the Vaganova diagonal line. Hence the two Vaganova arabesques in which a single arm is extended in front on the opposite side of the body from the raised leg are the 1st and the 3rd arabesques, the en ligne / croisé arabesques.

4.text:
PRIVATE REFLECTION: The question is about the Vaganova derrière arabesques and which two have a single arm extended in front on the side opposite the lifted leg, i.e. the classic épaulement croisé / contralateral port de bras.

Current round 1 public positions have shifted relative to round 0.

* B. Second and third is now the largest bloc in round 1: Colleagues 11,13,14,16,17,19,2,21,5,7,9 plus supporting arguments from 13,14,16. Claim: Arabesque I in Vaganova is the basic symmetrical / en face position, taught with arms in open seconde / no clear forward arm, or with both arms together in front, so it does not meet the “arm extended in front” criterion. Arabesque II is the classic profile opposition / croisé: working leg derrière, torso in profile/effacé, the arm on the supporting/standing leg carried forward in front of the torso and the arm on the working-leg side carried back on the line of the leg. The forward arm is therefore contralateral/opposite the lifted leg. Arabesque III keeps that same contralateral principle as a continuation / more open/lyrical/cambré version of II: leg still derrière, forward arm still on the supporting side opposite the working leg, back arm on the line of the leg, arms worked a little higher/rounder. Arabesque IV is the closed/crossed finish: arms brought together in high fifth/low first / closed cambré, same-side carriage, no single clear forward-opposite arm. Hence II + III are the two with a forward arm opposite the leg.

* C. First and third remains a coherent minority: Colleagues 1,3,4,8. Claim: Vaganova odd numbers = opposition, even numbers = same-side. Arabesque I = en ligne/profile opposition with one arm forward on the standing-leg side opposite the lifted leg and one arm back on the lifted-leg side. Arabesque III = same opposition principle higher/open/cambré, forward arm still opposite the lifted leg. Arabesque II and IV = same-side variants where the forward arm is on the same side as the lifted leg. They interpret Arabesque I as having a straight arabesque line with one arm forward/one back, not arms in seconde.

* E. Second and fourth is a second minority: Colleagues 10,12,15,18,20,6. Claim: Arabesque I = arms in seconde/no front arm. Arabesque II = open opposition with forward arm opposite the lifted leg. Arabesque III = closed/lyrical both-arms-in-front / same-side, no single opposite forward arm. Arabesque IV = finished/inclined form of the opposition, forward arm again opposite the lifted leg. Hence II + IV.

Key points of disagreement persisting from round 0:
- What Arabesque I actually is in Vaganova: arms in second/no front arm vs straight arabesque line with one arm forward one back in opposition.
- What Arabesque III actually is: opposition with forward arm opposite vs both arms brought forward/closed lyrical line / same-side.
- What Arabesque IV actually is: continuation of II opposition with forward arm opposite vs closed/same-side/fifth.

Evidence cited is all about port de bras, épaulement croisé, diagonal line, no external canonical source quoted. The split clearly hinges on differing numbering/translations of Vaganova’s four arabesques between Russian syllabus description and French/Italian teaching tradition.

My own belief remains unsettled but is moving toward the B. Second and third interpretation because it is now the majority in round 1 and it provides a consistent mapping: I = symmetrical base with no isolated forward arm; II = textbook contralateral opposition; III = continuation of II with the same contralateral forward arm but more open/lyrical; IV = closed finish losing the single forward-opposite line. The C mapping relies on an odd=opposition/even=same-side scheme that conflicts with the widely repeated claim in round 1 that Vaganova I is arms in seconde. The E mapping relies on III being closed both-arms-in-front, which is disputed by the B bloc who argue III retains the contralateral forward arm.

Unresolved: need a reliable canonical mapping of Vaganova I-IV to port de bras. The core diagnostic to resolve is whether Vaganova Arabesque I is taught with a single forward arm at all, and whether Arabesque III preserves the contralateral forward arm or becomes closed. Until that is clarified, C, B and E remain plausible under different numbering conventions.

3.text:
PRIVATE REFLECTION: The question is about the Vaganova port de bras with the working leg en arabesque derrière and which two arabesques show a single arm carried en avant on the supporting/standing leg side, i.e. contralateral/opposite to the lifted leg. The core concept – opposition = forward arm on standing leg side opposite lifted leg; same-side = forward arm on lifted leg side – is agreed, the dispute is the Vaganova numbering of the four positions.

Three mappings are in play:

* C camp – en ligne/opposition pair = I & III, same-side pair = II & IV. Arabesque I is upright opposition en profile/en face with one arm en avant on the standing leg side opposite the lifted leg and one arm en arrière on the line of the lifted leg; Arabesque III is the cambré/inclined continuation of the same opposition, forward arm still contralateral. II and IV have the forward arm on the same side as the lifted leg. This was the majority detailed syllabus citation in round 0 and is still argued by Colleagues 1,3,4,8 in round 1.

* B camp – contralateral forward-arm pair = II & III, I = arms in seconde/symmetrical no clear forward arm, IV = closed/same-side. Arabesque II is the classic profile épaulement croisé with the free arm forward in front of the torso on the opposite side to the lifted leg and the supporting arm back; Arabesque III keeps that same contralateral opposition with a more open/lyrical/cambré arm shape and the forward arm still on the opposite side to the leg. Arabesque I is taught as arms in open second / en face symmetrical, Arabesque IV closes to a high fifth/crossed/same-side carriage. This is now the largest block in round 1: Colleagues 11,13,14,16,17,19,2,21,5,7,9.

* E camp – open opposition pair = II & IV, I = arms in seconde, III = closed both-arms-in-front. Arabesque II is upright opposition with forward arm contralateral; Arabesque IV is the inclined/cambré form of the same opposition. Arabesque I has no forward arm and Arabesque III is the closed lyrical both-arms-forward/same-side variation. Argued by Colleagues 10,12,15,18,20,6 in round 1.

Instability is visible: Colleague 1 moved E → C between rounds, Colleague 10 moved C → E, showing numbering sensitivity.

Unresolved points remain: the exact description of Arabesque III – whether it retains the same opposition as I/II with a single contralateral forward arm, or is described as arms brought together in front/cambré with no single forward opposition – and the definition of Arabesque I – en ligne opposition with one arm avant/one arrière versus arms in second with no projected forward arm. Different pedagogical sources number the en ligne vs croisé variants differently, producing the C vs B shift.

Current weight of round 1 detailed port de bras citations favors the B mapping: II as classic opposition and III as its continuation, with I as symmetrical arms in second and IV as closed. The C mapping remains plausible if one adopts the en ligne = I & III, croisé = II & IV numbering convention. Need a definitive Vaganova source confirming the official numbering of en ligne vs croisé and the exact arm carriage for III to resolve the tie.

10.text:
PRIVATE REFLECTION: The deliberation remains split on Vaganova numbering / port de bras mapping, with a clear shift in the current round toward B Second and third.

Current round counts: B Second and third is now the plurality/majority: Colleagues 11,13,14,16,17,19,2,21,5,7,9 argue II is classic opposition/croisé with working leg derrière, torso in profile/effacé, forward arm carried in front on the supporting / standing side i.e. opposite the lifted leg, back arm on line of lifted leg. III is presented as the continuation/open/cambré/lyrical version of that same opposition: leg still derrière, torso a little more ouvert/cambré, forward-projected arm remains contralateral on supporting side opposite lifted leg, back arm remains on line of leg. Arabesque I is described as symmetrical/en face/arms in open seconde with no clearly projected forward arm, and Arabesque IV is described as closed/high fifth/both arms together/same-side finish where the clear single forward-opposite arm is lost.

C First and third minority persists: Colleagues 1,3,4,8 argue Arabesque I is the upright en ligne/opposition arabesque with one arm en avant on standing side opposite lifted leg and one arm en arrière on line of lifted leg; Arabesque III is the inclined/cambré counterpart retaining that same opposition. Arabesques II and IV are the same-side/ipsilateral variants where forward arm is on same side as lifted leg. This view treats I as one-arm-forward-opposite, not arms in second.

E Second and fourth minority persists: Colleagues 10,12,15,18,20,6 argue Arabesque I is arms in open seconde/no forward arm; Arabesque III is closed/lyrical both-arms-forward/cambré with no single contrasted forward arm. The open opposition family is II upright and IV inclined/cambré, both with forward arm on supporting side opposite lifted leg, back arm on line of leg. This view treats III as closed/same-side and IV as the finished opposition.

Core disagreements unchanged:
* Is Arabesque I arms in second with no forward arm, or one arm forward one back with forward arm opposite? B/E camps say no forward arm; C camp says forward arm opposite.
* Is Arabesque III a both-arms-in-front closed cambré with no single opposite forward arm, or the open continuation of II with forward arm still opposite? E camp says closed; B camp says continuation of opposition; C camp also says opposite.
* Is Arabesque IV same-side/closed or the inclined open opposition mirroring II? C camp says same-side; E camp says open opposition; B camp says closed.

Evidence that is now robust across most detailed anatomical descriptions: the classic Vaganova épaulement croisé with a single arm extended in front on the side opposite the lifted leg is unequivocally II. The partner position is contested between III and IV depending on numbering convention.

My current belief is leaning to the majority B Second and third interpretation: II is the textbook contralateral forward arm, III keeps that contralateral principle in a more open/lyrical shape, I is the symmetrical arms-in-seconde base, and IV closes the arms. The C First and third and E Second and fourth views remain plausible due to naming convention variability and persistent conflicting textbook descriptions of I and III/IV.

Unresolved: exact Vaganova syllabus definition of Arabesque I port de bras and whether III is the open lyrical continuation of II or the closed both-arms-forward position, and whether IV is the inclined opposition or the closed finish.

PRIVATE REFLECTION: The deliberation remains dominated by numbering convention, not by the anatomy of the port de bras.

Round 0 already showed three camps: odd = opposition → First and Third; I = arms in second, II/III = opposition → Second and Third; open opposition = II and IV → Second and Fourth. The core principle repeatedly invoked is opposition vs same-side and the Vaganova diagonal with a single forward arm on the supporting-leg side, i.e. opposite the lifted leg.

Round 1 public responses shift the weight of the discussion. 

Second and Third camp is now the largest. Colleagues 11,13,14,16,17,19,2,21,5,7,9 describe Vaganova Arabesque I as symmetrical / arms in seconde / en face with no clearly projected forward arm. Arabesque II is the classic profile opposition/croisé: working leg derrière, torso in profile/effacé, arm on standing side carried forward in front of the torso and arm on working-leg side carried back on the line of the leg. That forward arm is contralateral, opposite the lifted leg. Arabesque III is presented as the continuation/opening/lyrical/cambré version of the same opposition: leg still derrière, torso a little more ouvert, forward arm still contralateral, back arm on the line of the leg. Arabesque IV is then the closed finish – arms together in high fifth/low first or same-side carriage, the clear single forward-opposite relationship lost.

First and Third camp persists with Colleagues 1,3,4,8. They map I and III as the opposition / en ligne arabesques with the forward arm on the standing-leg side opposite the lifted leg, and II and IV as same-side. Their description matches the odd = opposite pattern and treats Arabesque I as the upright opposition with one arm en avant / one en arrière, not arms in seconde.

Second and Fourth camp persists with Colleagues 10,12,15,18,20,6. They map I = arms in seconde / no forward arm, III = closed both-arms-in-front lyrical, and II and IV as the upright and inclined open opposition with the forward arm opposite the lifted leg.

I previously leaned to First and Third based on the odd opposition reading. The current round evidence, especially the detailed port-de-bras descriptions for how Vaganova is actually taught in syllabus texts, pushes me toward the Second and Third reading. The key discriminating fact is whether Arabesque I in the question’s numbering is the arms-in-seconde base position with no isolated forward arm. If I is arms in seconde, then a forward arm opposite the leg cannot be First; it must start at II, and the continuation is III.

Unresolved: the alternative numbering where the basic opposition is labelled I and the arms-in-seconde position is labelled II. That convention explains the First and Third supporters and the odd/even alternation they cite. Without an explicit source citation for the question’s numbering, the risk of a convention mismatch remains.

Current best estimate: the intended answer under the commonly taught Vaganova syllabus mapping is B. Second and third, with the caveat that a First and Third answer reflects the same anatomical principle under a different numbering convention.

20.text:
PRIVATE REFLECTION: The numbering disagreement persists but the balance of detailed port de bras descriptions in round 1 has shifted toward the II/III pair.

The three live camps remain:

* I/III camp – Arabesque I and III are the opposition / en ligne croisé arabesques, upright and cambré respectively, with the forward arm on the supporting/standing side, i.e. opposite the lifted leg. Arabesques II and IV are the same-side/ipsilateral variants with the forward arm on the same side as the lifted leg. Colleagues 1, 3, 4, 8 hold this in round 1, and Colleague 1 flipped from E to C this round.
* II/IV camp – Arabesque I is arms in second/no forward arm, Arabesque III is closed/both-arms-in-front lyrical, while II is the upright opposition croisé and IV is the inclined/cambré continuation of that same opposition. Both have a single arm carried in front on the supporting side opposite the lifted leg. Colleagues 10,12,15,18,20,6 hold this in round 1.
* II/III camp – Arabesque I is symmetrical arms in second / en face with no clearly projected forward arm; Arabesque IV is a closed/high fifth / same-side finish. Arabesque II is the classic profile opposition with the free arm forward on the opposite side to the lifted leg and the other arm back on the line of the leg; Arabesque III keeps that same contralateral principle with a more open/lyrical/cambré arm shape and torso, the forward-projected arm still contralateral to the working leg. This is the current majority in round 1: Colleagues 11,13,14,16,17,19,2,21,5,7,9.

Key evidence repeatedly cited for II/III: Vaganova numbers arabesques by port de bras with the leg en arrière. The defining épaulement croisé is a single arm en avant on the standing side and arm en arrière on the working-leg side. II is the textbook upright profile opposition. III is taught as its continuation/opening, not as a closed both-arms-in-front position, and the forward arm remains contralateral. I is described as basic open second / en face with no isolated forward arm; IV is described as closed/high fifth/crossed with the clear forward-opposite line lost.

Key evidence for I/III: odd numbers = opposition, even numbers = same-side. I is upright opposition, III is inclined opposition, the forward arm is on the supporting side opposite the lifted leg. II and IV have the forward arm on the same side as the lifted leg.

Key evidence for II/IV: I is arms in second, III is closed lyrical both-arms-in-front, II is upright opposition, IV is inclined opposition, upright II and inclined IV share the same front-opposite arm relationship.

Unresolved that drives the split is the mapping of Vaganova’s first arabesque between “arms in second / no forward arm” versus “first croisé opposition”, and whether Arabesque III is the open contralateral continuation of II or the closed both-arms-in-front lyrical line. The anatomical requirement of a single arm actually extended in front makes the “arms in second” reading of I implausible for a front-arm criterion, and the pairing of an upright opposition with its inclined counterpart is anatomically consistent.

Current weight of detailed port-de-bras arguments in this round pushes me toward the Second-and-Third opposition pair, option B, with the caveat that textbooks differ in numbering and the I/III labeling is the mirror of the same opposition principle in some pedagogies. The II/IV camp remains a strong minority with coherent Vaganova syllabus arguments, and the I/III camp remains coherent under an alternative numbering convention.

Arabesque II is the classic profile opposition/épaulement croisé: working leg derrière, torso in profile, arm on standing side carried forward in front of torso on side opposite lifted leg, back arm on line of lifted leg. Arabesque III keeps the same contralateral intention, described as the continuation/open/lyrical/cambré development of II: leg still derrière, torso a little more ouvert/cambré, arms higher/rounder, but forward-projected arm remains the contralateral arm on supporting side opposite working leg with back arm on line of leg. Arabesque IV closes the line – arms brought together in high fifth/low first/crossed devant, more same-side/gathered carriage, clear single forward-opposite arm lost.

* E. Second and fourth – 6 colleagues: 10,12,15,18,20,6.
Core claim: I is basic en face/high second, arms to sides, no arm carried in front. II is first upright opposition croisé with forward arm on supporting side opposite lifted leg, back arm on line of leg. III is the closed/lyrical line: arms brought together in front in first/low first/cambré, no single contrasted forward arm in opposition, often described as same-side/closed. IV is the inclined/cambré finished form of the opposition: same croisé port de bras as II – forward arm on supporting side opposite lifted leg, back arm on line of leg – now with épaulement and slight torso inclination. Hence the open opposition pair is II + IV.

* C. First and third – 4 colleagues: 1,3,4,8.
Core claim: odd = opposition, even = same-side. Arabesque I en ligne/profile opposition: straight arabesque line one arm en avant one en arrière, forward arm on supporting leg side opposite lifted leg. Arabesque III is the high/inclined/cambré counterpart of I, still keeping the opposition line with forward arm on standing side opposite lifted leg. Arabesques II and IV are the same-side/ipsilateral variants where the forward arm is on same side as lifted leg.

Important claims and evidence persisting:
- Port de bras, not leg height, distinguishes the four derrière arabesques.
- Épaulement croisé is the defining Vaganova aesthetic for the contralateral line.
- Arabesque I: split. B/E camps now largely converge that I is taught with arms in seconde/symmetrical and has no distinct single forward arm. C camp still describes I as a straight en ligne opposition with one arm forward opposite lifted leg.
- Arabesque III: central dispute. B camp says III keeps II’s contralateral forward arm, just with a more open/lyrical/cambré shape. E camp says III is closed/both-arms-in-front lyrical cambré with no single opposed forward arm, and that the forward-opposite line moves to IV.
- Arabesque IV: B camp says IV closes to high fifth/crossed and loses the clear forward-opposite relationship; E camp says IV is the inclined continuation of II’s opposition.

Change in belief: Round-0 was unsettled C ~8, B ~9, E ~3. Round-1 distribution is B 11, E 6, C 4, with a clear shift away from the First-and-Third odd/even pairing and toward rejection of a forward arm in Arabesque I. The description of I as arms in second with no single forward arm is now the majority position.

Unresolved: canonical Vaganova syllabus numbering for port de bras of III vs IV; whether “arm extended in front” means a single distinct projected forward arm or a general forward placement; and the precise textbook wording for III as contralateral continuation vs closed lyrical line.

Current working understanding leans toward B Second and Third as the most coherent majority account in this round: I has no single forward arm, II has the classic contralateral forward arm, III preserves that contralateral forward arm in a more open/lyrical shape, IV closes the arms and no longer shows the clear single forward-opposite line.

reflection_text.4:
The question is about the Vaganova derrière arabesques and which two have a single arm extended in front on the side opposite the lifted leg, i.e. the classic épaulement croisé / contralateral port de bras.

Current round 1 public positions have shifted relative to round 0.

* B. Second and third is now the largest bloc in round 1: Colleagues 11,13,14,16,17,19,2,21,5,7,9 plus supporting arguments from 13,14,16. Claim: Arabesque I in Vaganova is the basic symmetrical / en face position, taught with arms in open seconde / no clear forward arm, or with both arms together in front, so it does not meet the “arm extended in front” criterion. Arabesque II is the classic profile opposition / croisé: working leg derrière, torso in profile/effacé, the arm on the supporting/standing leg carried forward in front of the torso and the arm on the working-leg side carried back on the line of the leg. The forward arm is therefore contralateral/opposite the lifted leg. Arabesque III keeps that same contralateral principle as a continuation / more open/lyrical/cambré version of II: leg still derrière, forward arm still on the supporting side opposite the working leg, back arm on the line of the leg, arms worked a little higher/rounder. Arabesque IV is the closed/crossed finish: arms brought together in high fifth/low first / closed cambré, same-side carriage, no single clear forward-opposite arm. Hence II + III are the two with a forward arm opposite the leg.

* C. First and third remains a coherent minority: Colleagues 1,3,4,8. Claim: Vaganova odd numbers = opposition, even numbers = same-side. Arabesque I = en ligne/profile opposition with one arm forward on the standing-leg side opposite the lifted leg and one arm back on the lifted-leg side. Arabesque III = same opposition principle higher/open/cambré, forward arm still opposite the lifted leg. Arabesque II and IV = same-side variants where the forward arm is on the same side as the lifted leg. They interpret Arabesque I as having a straight arabesque line with one arm forward/one back, not arms in seconde.

* E. Second and fourth is a second minority: Colleagues 10,12,15,18,20,6. Claim: Arabesque I = arms in seconde/no front arm. Arabesque II = open opposition with forward arm opposite the lifted leg. Arabesque III = closed/lyrical both-arms-in-front / same-side, no single opposite forward arm. Arabesque IV = finished/inclined form of the opposition, forward arm again opposite the lifted leg. Hence II + IV.

Key points of disagreement persisting from round 0:
- What Arabesque I actually is in Vaganova: arms in second/no front arm vs straight arabesque line with one arm forward one back in opposition.
- What Arabesque III actually is: opposition with forward arm opposite vs both arms brought forward/closed lyrical line / same-side.
- What Arabesque IV actually is: continuation of II opposition with forward arm opposite vs closed/same-side/fifth.

Evidence cited is all about port de bras, épaulement croisé, diagonal line, no external canonical source quoted. The split clearly hinges on differing numbering/translations of Vaganova’s four arabesques between Russian syllabus description and French/Italian teaching tradition.

My own belief remains unsettled but is moving toward the B. Second and third interpretation because it is now the majority in round 1 and it provides a consistent mapping: I = symmetrical base with no isolated forward arm; II = textbook contralateral opposition; III = continuation of II with the same contralateral forward arm but more open/lyrical; IV = closed finish losing the single forward-opposite line. The C mapping relies on an odd=opposition/even=same-side scheme that conflicts with the widely repeated claim in round 1 that Vaganova I is arms in seconde. The E mapping relies on III being closed both-arms-in-front, which is disputed by the B bloc who argue III retains the contralateral forward arm.

Unresolved: need a reliable canonical mapping of Vaganova I-IV to port de bras. The core diagnostic to resolve is whether Vaganova Arabesque I is taught with a single forward arm at all, and whether Arabesque III preserves the contralateral forward arm or becomes closed. Until that is clarified, C, B and E remain plausible under different numbering conventions.
reflection_text.3:
The question is about the Vaganova port de bras with the working leg en arabesque derrière and which two arabesques show a single arm carried en avant on the supporting/standing leg side, i.e. contralateral/opposite to the lifted leg. The core concept – opposition = forward arm on standing leg side opposite lifted leg; same-side = forward arm on lifted leg side – is agreed, the dispute is the Vaganova numbering of the four positions.

Three mappings are in play:

* C camp – en ligne/opposition pair = I & III, same-side pair = II & IV. Arabesque I is upright opposition en profile/en face with one arm en avant on the standing leg side opposite the lifted leg and one arm en arrière on the line of the lifted leg; Arabesque III is the cambré/inclined continuation of the same opposition, forward arm still contralateral. II and IV have the forward arm on the same side as the lifted leg. This was the majority detailed syllabus citation in round 0 and is still argued by Colleagues 1,3,4,8 in round 1.

* B camp – contralateral forward-arm pair = II & III, I = arms in seconde/symmetrical no clear forward arm, IV = closed/same-side. Arabesque II is the classic profile épaulement croisé with the free arm forward in front of the torso on the opposite side to the lifted leg and the supporting arm back; Arabesque III keeps that same contralateral opposition with a more open/lyrical/cambré arm shape and the forward arm still on the opposite side to the leg. Arabesque I is taught as arms in open second / en face symmetrical, Arabesque IV closes to a high fifth/crossed/same-side carriage. This is now the largest block in round 1: Colleagues 11,13,14,16,17,19,2,21,5,7,9.

* E camp – open opposition pair = II & IV, I = arms in seconde, III = closed both-arms-in-front. Arabesque II is upright opposition with forward arm contralateral; Arabesque IV is the inclined/cambré form of the same opposition. Arabesque I has no forward arm and Arabesque III is the closed lyrical both-arms-forward/same-side variation. Argued by Colleagues 10,12,15,18,20,6 in round 1.

Instability is visible: Colleague 1 moved E → C between rounds, Colleague 10 moved C → E, showing numbering sensitivity.

Unresolved points remain: the exact description of Arabesque III – whether it retains the same opposition as I/II with a single contralateral forward arm, or is described as arms brought together in front/cambré with no single forward opposition – and the definition of Arabesque I – en ligne opposition with one arm avant/one arrière versus arms in second with no projected forward arm. Different pedagogical sources number the en ligne vs croisé variants differently, producing the C vs B shift.

Current weight of round 1 detailed port de bras citations favors the B mapping: II as classic opposition and III as its continuation, with I as symmetrical arms in second and IV as closed. The C mapping remains plausible if one adopts the en ligne = I & III, croisé = II & IV numbering convention. Need a definitive Vaganova source confirming the official numbering of en ligne vs croisé and the exact arm carriage for III to resolve the tie.
reflection_text.10:
The deliberation remains split on Vaganova numbering / port de bras mapping, with a clear shift in the current round toward B Second and third.

Current round counts: B Second and third is now the plurality/majority: Colleagues 11,13,14,16,17,19,2,21,5,7,9 argue II is classic opposition/croisé with working leg derrière, torso in profile/effacé, forward arm carried in front on the supporting / standing side i.e. opposite the lifted leg, back arm on line of lifted leg. III is presented as the continuation/open/cambré/lyrical version of that same opposition: leg still derrière, torso a little more ouvert/cambré, forward-projected arm remains contralateral on supporting side opposite lifted leg, back arm remains on line of leg. Arabesque I is described as symmetrical/en face/arms in open seconde with no clearly projected forward arm, and Arabesque IV is described as closed/high fifth/both arms together/same-side finish where the clear single forward-opposite arm is lost.

C First and third minority persists: Colleagues 1,3,4,8 argue Arabesque I is the upright en ligne/opposition arabesque with one arm en avant on standing side opposite lifted leg and one arm en arrière on line of lifted leg; Arabesque III is the inclined/cambré counterpart retaining that same opposition. Arabesques II and IV are the same-side/ipsilateral variants where forward arm is on same side as lifted leg. This view treats I as one-arm-forward-opposite, not arms in second.

E Second and fourth minority persists: Colleagues 10,12,15,18,20,6 argue Arabesque I is arms in open seconde/no forward arm; Arabesque III is closed/lyrical both-arms-forward/cambré with no single contrasted forward arm. The open opposition family is II upright and IV inclined/cambré, both with forward arm on supporting side opposite lifted leg, back arm on line of leg. This view treats III as closed/same-side and IV as the finished opposition.

Core disagreements unchanged:
* Is Arabesque I arms in second with no forward arm, or one arm forward one back with forward arm opposite? B/E camps say no forward arm; C camp says forward arm opposite.
* Is Arabesque III a both-arms-in-front closed cambré with no single opposite forward arm, or the open continuation of II with forward arm still opposite? E camp says closed; B camp says continuation of opposition; C camp also says opposite.
* Is Arabesque IV same-side/closed or the inclined open opposition mirroring II? C camp says same-side; E camp says open opposition; B camp says closed.

Evidence that is now robust across most detailed anatomical descriptions: the classic Vaganova épaulement croisé with a single arm extended in front on the side opposite the lifted leg is unequivocally II. The partner position is contested between III and IV depending on numbering convention.

My current belief is leaning to the majority B Second and third interpretation: II is the textbook contralateral forward arm, III keeps that contralateral principle in a more open/lyrical shape, I is the symmetrical arms-in-seconde base, and IV closes the arms. The C First and third and E Second and fourth views remain plausible due to naming convention variability and persistent conflicting textbook descriptions of I and III/IV.

Unresolved: exact Vaganova syllabus definition of Arabesque I port de bras and whether III is the open lyrical continuation of II or the closed both-arms-forward position, and whether IV is the inclined opposition or the closed finish.
reflection_text.11:
The debate remains about Vaganova arabesque numbering vs port de bras mapping, but the distribution shifted in round 1.

* Camps now visible
  * B. Second and third – majority in round 1: Colleagues 11,13,14,16,17,19,2,21,5,7,9. Argument: Vaganova I = symmetrical / arms in open second, en face, no clearly projected forward arm. II = classic profile opposition / croisé: working leg derrière, torso effacé, arm on standing side carried forward in front of torso i.e. opposite the lifted leg, back arm on line of lifted leg. III = continuation of II with more open/cambré/lyrical arm shape and slightly more ouvert torso, but the contralateral forward arm relationship is preserved: forward arm still on supporting side opposite the lifted leg, back arm on line of leg. IV = closed finish: arms brought together in high fifth / crossed / both-arms-in-front, no longer a single clear forward-opposite arm.
  * E. Second and fourth – Colleagues 10,12,15,18,20,6. Argument: I = basic upright, arms in open second, no forward arm. II = first open opposition with forward arm on supporting side opposite lifted leg. III = closed lyrical / both arms forward / same-side, no single contrasted forward arm. IV = inclined/cambré version of the same opposition as II: forward arm still on supporting side opposite lifted leg, back arm on line of leg. So forward-opposite arm = II and IV.
  * C. First and third – Colleagues 1,3,4,8. Argument: Vaganova opposition pair is I and III. I = en ligne / upright opposition, one arm en avant on standing-leg side opposite lifted leg, one arm en arrière on line of lifted leg. III = high/inclined/cambré counterpart of I, same opposition retained: forward arm still on standing side opposite lifted leg. II and IV are same-side / ipsilateral variants where forward arm is on same side as lifted leg.

* Evidence and contradictions carried over
  * Definition of Arabesque I is the pivot: B/E camps say I = arms in seconde / symmetrical, no forward arm. C camp says I = en ligne with forward arm on opposite side. The same split existed in round 0.
  * Definition of Arabesque III is contested: B camp says III keeps contralateral opposition, more lyrical shape. E camp says III is closed both-arms-in-front / same-side. C camp says III is open counterpart of I with opposition retained.
  * Definition of Arabesque IV is contested: E camp says IV is inclined opposition with forward arm opposite. B camp says IV closes arms / high fifth, forward-opposite lost. C camp says IV is same-side with forward arm on same side as leg.
  * Some colleagues explicitly note the confusion between Vaganova syllabus numbering and classroom shorthand where arabesque I is sometimes taught as en ligne.

* What remains unresolved
  * Which numbering convention the question assumes – syllabus numbering where I = arms in second, or a pedagogic numbering where I = en ligne opposition.
  * Whether “arm extended in front” means a single clearly forward-projected arm vs a diagonal arm line.
  * The port de bras for III and IV: whether III retains opposition or closes, and whether IV is the inclined opposition or a closed same-side finish.

Current leaning: B Second and third now has numerical majority in round 1 and is internally coherent with the standard Vaganova description that I is arms in second with no forward arm, II is classic croisé opposition, III is its lyrical continuation. The C First and third view is detailed and repeated, but depends on interpreting Arabesque I as en ligne with a forward arm, which conflicts with the syllabus description given by the B/E camps. E Second and fourth is plausible if IV is taken as the inclined opposition, but then III must be closed, which is contradicted by many B descriptions. No definitive source cited; need a reliable authoritative mapping of Vaganova I–IV port de bras to resolve the I definition and the III/IV distinction.
reflection_text.6:
The round-1 public set remains split on the numbering of the Vaganova port de bras, but the discussion has converged on a few stable points and the disagreement has narrowed to III vs IV.

* Stable agreement: the defining feature is a forward-carried arm on the supporting/standing side, i.e. opposite the working leg behind, with the other arm carried back on the line of the lifted leg. No one disputes that Arabesque II is the classic croisé/opposition arabesque with a clear contralateral front arm. Arabesque I is now widely described in this round as an en face/symmetrical position with the arms in an open seconde / no single arm carried in front. That eliminates any option containing I, e.g. A. First and second, C. First and third.

* Where the split remains is the fate of Arabesque III and Arabesque IV.

  - II + III camp – colleagues 11,13,14,16,17,19,2,21,5,7,9 and similar: I = arms in seconde, no forward arm. II = classic profile opposition, front arm opposite the lifted leg. III keeps that same contralateral opposition, more open/lyrical/cambré, with the front arm still projected in front on the supporting side opposite the working leg, back arm on the line of the leg. IV is the closed/finished position: arms brought together in a high fifth/low first or same-side carriage, the clear single forward-opposite line is lost. Hence the answer is B. Second and third.

  - II + IV camp – colleagues 10,12,15,18,20,6 and similar: I = arms in seconde, no forward arm. II = upright opposition, front arm opposite the leg. III = closed/lyrical both-arms-in-front or same-side cambré line, no single contrasted forward arm opposite the leg. IV = finished/inclined form of the opposition, preserving the same croisé port de bras as II with the front arm still on the supporting side opposite the lifted leg, now with épaulement and a slight torso inclination. Hence the answer is E. Second and fourth.

* First and third camp persists with colleagues 1,3,4,8. They now assert Arabesque I is an upright opposition with a forward arm opposite the leg and Arabesque III is the cambré continuation of that opposition, while II and IV are same-side. This is increasingly inconsistent with the dominant current claim that I is taught with the arms in seconde and has no forward arm.

Changes from round 0:
- The no-forward-arm-in-I claim is now dominant in the current round, weakening C. First and third.
- Colleague 1 flipped from E to C, Colleague 10 flipped from C to E, Colleague 12 flipped from B to E. The II + III majority has grown relative to round 0.
- The core contradiction remains the description of Arabesque III: same opposition as II with a more open/lyrical shape vs closed both-arms-in-front/ same-side lyrical position. The description of Arabesque IV mirrors this: finished opposition vs closed/high fifth.

Current belief update:
With I effectively ruled out by the “arms in seconde, no forward arm” consensus, II is uncontroversial. The weight of the current round favors the II + III pairing: majority of colleagues now argue III retains the contralateral forward arm and IV is the closed/finished position. The II + IV argument remains plausible and well-argued, especially on the claim that III is the both-arms-forward lyrical arabesque and IV is the inclined opposition. The unresolved question is authoritative syllabus confirmation of the exact port de bras for III versus IV, because the literature is quoted both ways in the discussion. I will keep II + III as the working best summary, with the II + IV counter-argument retained as the main alternative pending verification of III’s arm placement.
reflection_text.8:
The deliberation remains dominated by numbering convention, not by the anatomy of the port de bras.

Round 0 already showed three camps: odd = opposition → First and Third; I = arms in second, II/III = opposition → Second and Third; open opposition = II and IV → Second and Fourth. The core principle repeatedly invoked is opposition vs same-side and the Vaganova diagonal with a single forward arm on the supporting-leg side, i.e. opposite the lifted leg.

Round 1 public responses shift the weight of the discussion. 

Second and Third camp is now the largest. Colleagues 11,13,14,16,17,19,2,21,5,7,9 describe Vaganova Arabesque I as symmetrical / arms in seconde / en face with no clearly projected forward arm. Arabesque II is the classic profile opposition/croisé: working leg derrière, torso in profile/effacé, arm on standing side carried forward in front of the torso and arm on working-leg side carried back on the line of the leg. That forward arm is contralateral, opposite the lifted leg. Arabesque III is presented as the continuation/opening/lyrical/cambré version of the same opposition: leg still derrière, torso a little more ouvert, forward arm still contralateral, back arm on the line of the leg. Arabesque IV is then the closed finish – arms together in high fifth/low first or same-side carriage, the clear single forward-opposite relationship lost.

First and Third camp persists with Colleagues 1,3,4,8. They map I and III as the opposition / en ligne arabesques with the forward arm on the standing-leg side opposite the lifted leg, and II and IV as same-side. Their description matches the odd = opposite pattern and treats Arabesque I as the upright opposition with one arm en avant / one en arrière, not arms in seconde.

Second and Fourth camp persists with Colleagues 10,12,15,18,20,6. They map I = arms in seconde / no forward arm, III = closed both-arms-in-front lyrical, and II and IV as the upright and inclined open opposition with the forward arm opposite the lifted leg.

I previously leaned to First and Third based on the odd opposition reading. The current round evidence, especially the detailed port-de-bras descriptions for how Vaganova is actually taught in syllabus texts, pushes me toward the Second and Third reading. The key discriminating fact is whether Arabesque I in the question’s numbering is the arms-in-seconde base position with no isolated forward arm. If I is arms in seconde, then a forward arm opposite the leg cannot be First; it must start at II, and the continuation is III.

Unresolved: the alternative numbering where the basic opposition is labelled I and the arms-in-seconde position is labelled II. That convention explains the First and Third supporters and the odd/even alternation they cite. Without an explicit source citation for the question’s numbering, the risk of a convention mismatch remains.

Current best estimate: the intended answer under the commonly taught Vaganova syllabus mapping is B. Second and third, with the caveat that a First and Third answer reflects the same anatomical principle under a different numbering convention.
reflection_text.20:
The numbering disagreement persists but the balance of detailed port de bras descriptions in round 1 has shifted toward the II/III pair.

The three live camps remain:

* I/III camp – Arabesque I and III are the opposition / en ligne croisé arabesques, upright and cambré respectively, with the forward arm on the supporting/standing side, i.e. opposite the lifted leg. Arabesques II and IV are the same-side/ipsilateral variants with the forward arm on the same side as the lifted leg. Colleagues 1, 3, 4, 8 hold this in round 1, and Colleague 1 flipped from E to C this round.
* II/IV camp – Arabesque I is arms in second/no forward arm, Arabesque III is closed/both-arms-in-front lyrical, while II is the upright opposition croisé and IV is the inclined/cambré continuation of that same opposition. Both have a single arm carried in front on the supporting side opposite the lifted leg. Colleagues 10,12,15,18,20,6 hold this in round 1.
* II/III camp – Arabesque I is symmetrical arms in second / en face with no clearly projected forward arm; Arabesque IV is a closed/high fifth / same-side finish. Arabesque II is the classic profile opposition with the free arm forward on the opposite side to the lifted leg and the other arm back on the line of the leg; Arabesque III keeps that same contralateral principle with a more open/lyrical/cambré arm shape and torso, the forward-projected arm still contralateral to the working leg. This is the current majority in round 1: Colleagues 11,13,14,16,17,19,2,21,5,7,9.

Key evidence repeatedly cited for II/III: Vaganova numbers arabesques by port de bras with the leg en arrière. The defining épaulement croisé is a single arm en avant on the standing side and arm en arrière on the working-leg side. II is the textbook upright profile opposition. III is taught as its continuation/opening, not as a closed both-arms-in-front position, and the forward arm remains contralateral. I is described as basic open second / en face with no isolated forward arm; IV is described as closed/high fifth/crossed with the clear forward-opposite line lost.

Key evidence for I/III: odd numbers = opposition, even numbers = same-side. I is upright opposition, III is inclined opposition, the forward arm is on the supporting side opposite the lifted leg. II and IV have the forward arm on the same side as the lifted leg.

Key evidence for II/IV: I is arms in second, III is closed lyrical both-arms-in-front, II is upright opposition, IV is inclined opposition, upright II and inclined IV share the same front-opposite arm relationship.

Unresolved that drives the split is the mapping of Vaganova’s first arabesque between “arms in second / no forward arm” versus “first croisé opposition”, and whether Arabesque III is the open contralateral continuation of II or the closed both-arms-in-front lyrical line. The anatomical requirement of a single arm actually extended in front makes the “arms in second” reading of I implausible for a front-arm criterion, and the pairing of an upright opposition with its inclined counterpart is anatomically consistent.

Current weight of detailed port-de-bras arguments in this round pushes me toward the Second-and-Third opposition pair, option B, with the caveat that textbooks differ in numbering and the I/III labeling is the mirror of the same opposition principle in some pedagogies. The II/IV camp remains a strong minority with coherent Vaganova syllabus arguments, and the I/III camp remains coherent under an alternative numbering convention.

reflection_text.1:
Round-0 was split with no consensus. The core dispute was the numbering offset for the Vaganova opposition / croisé port de bras where the arm carried in front is on the side of the supporting/standing leg i.e. opposite the lifted leg. The anatomical reality is stable: the contralateral forward-arm line is the Vaganova épaulement croisé diagonal; the disagreement is which numbers are mapped to it.

Round-1 public set has shifted. B. Second and third now has a clear plurality/majority: Colleagues 11,13,14,16,17,19,2,21,5,7,9 argue Vaganova I is the symmetrical / arms-in-seconde / en face base with no clearly projected forward arm, II is the classic profile opposition with the free arm extended forward on the opposite side to the lifted leg and the supporting arm back on the line of the leg, III keeps that same contralateral opposition with a more open/cambré arm shape and torso, and IV closes the arms in a high fifth / both-arms-in-front / same-side carriage. Third is essentially unanimously placed in the “forward arm opposite” group across camps.

C. First and third retains support from Colleagues 1,3,4,8. Their mapping is I = upright opposition, II = same-side upright, III = opposite cambré, IV = same-side cambré. They explicitly describe the odd-numbered arabesques as the opposition family and the even-numbered as the same-side family. This matches the traditional Russian pedagogical description in some texts where the numbers start with the opposition line.

E. Second and fourth is held by Colleagues 10,12,15,18,20,6. They treat I as arms in seconde / no forward arm, III as closed / both-arms-in-front lyrical, and II and IV as the two open opposition variations – upright II and inclined/cambré IV – with the forward arm opposite the lifted leg.

Important recurring evidence kept in both rounds:
* The four arabesques are defined by port de bras and épaulement, not leg height alone.
* Opposition = forward arm on supporting side opposite lifted leg, back arm on line of lifted leg.
* Third arabesque is almost universally cited as having the contralateral forward extension; the only disagreement is the partner number.
* The “I = arms in seconde, no forward arm” vs “I = upright opposition” reading is the source of the numbering offset.

Unresolved question remains the numbering convention: whether Vaganova’s “first” arabesque in the English syllabus is taught as arms in seconde with no isolated forward arm, or as the classic straight-line opposition croisé. Under the English syllabus convention used by the majority in Round-1, the clear single-arm-extended-in-front-on-the-opposite-side configuration is taught as Arabesque II and Arabesque III, with I being symmetrical and IV closed.

My current best synthesis updates from the Round-0 leaning toward C to a Round-1 leaning toward B. The contralateral forward-arm reality is agreed; given the majority of colleagues in Round-1 and the most common English Vaganova syllabus description where I = arms in seconde, the intended mapping for the question as phrased is most plausibly Second and Third. C. First and third remains defensible under the alternative Russian numbering where the opposition family is numbered 1/3, and the E. Second and fourth view misplaces III as closed. Pending confirmation of numbering convention, B is now the most parsimonious live consensus, with third arabesque as the stable anchor in the opposite-forward group.

B. Second and third claims:
* Arabesque I is symmetrical / arms in seconde / en face with no clearly projected forward arm, or arms together in a low first/second line.
* Arabesque II is the classic profile opposition / croisé: working leg derrière, torso in profile/effacé, free arm taken forward in front of torso on the side of the supporting leg i.e. opposite the lifted leg, supporting-side arm back on the line of the leg.
* Arabesque III keeps that same contralateral opposition principle, just with a more open / lyrical / cambré arm shape and slightly more opened torso; the forward-projected arm remains contralateral to the working leg, back arm on the line of the leg.
* Arabesque IV closes the line, arms brought together in high fifth / first / same-side carriage, no longer a single clear forward-opposite arm.

E. Second and fourth claims:

* Arabesque II = first open opposition, forward arm contralateral to lifted leg.
* Arabesque III = closed / lyrical / both-arms-in-front / cambré line, no single contrasted forward arm in opposition; some describe III as same-side forward arm.
* Arabesque IV = finished/inclined form of the same opposition as II, torso inclined forward but port de bras remains croisé: forward arm on supporting side opposite lifted leg, back arm on line of leg.

Representative: Colleague 10,12,15,18,20,6 describe II and IV as the open opposition pair and III as closed both-arms-forward.

C. First and third claims:
* Arabesque I and III are the opposition / en ligne arabesques: torso in profile/effacé, working leg derrière, forward arm on side of standing leg opposite lifted leg, back arm on line of lifted leg.

reflection_text.18:
The numbering/definition split persists and is now sharpened by round 1.

Core claims still in play:

* E. Second and fourth = open opposition. I is arms in seconde/no forward arm; II is upright contralateral opposition with the arm carried in front on the supporting/standing side i.e. opposite the lifted leg and the other arm back on the line of the leg; III is closed/lyrical both-arms-in-front/cambré with no single contralateral forward arm; IV is the inclined/cambré form of the same II opposition – forward arm still on the supporting side opposite the lifted leg, back arm on the line of the leg. Colleagues 10,12,15,18,20,6 give this detailed upright vs inclined mapping.

* C. First and third = odd-number opposition. I is upright en ligne/opposition with forward arm on the supporting side opposite the lifted leg, back arm on the line of the leg; III is the inclined/open version of the same opposition with the forward arm still opposite the lifted leg; II and IV are same-side/aligned variants where the forward arm is on the same side as the lifted leg. Colleagues 1,3,4,8 maintain this odd=opposition, even=same-side pattern.

* B. Second and third = I arms in seconde, II and III contralateral. I is symmetrical arms in seconde/en face with no isolated forward arm; II is classic profile opposition with forward arm opposite the lifted leg; III keeps that same contralateral principle, now more open/lyrical/cambré but still with the forward-projected arm on the supporting side opposite the lifted leg; IV closes the arms to a high fifth/crossed/same-side finish. Colleagues 11,13,14,16,17,19,2,21,5,7,9 argue this, making B the plurality in round 1.

Unresolved drivers:

* Whether Arabesque I is arms in seconde with no front arm or the first en ligne/opposition arabesque. That offset drives the I/II and III/IV swaps.
* How Arabesque III is defined: closed both-arms-in-front lyrical/cambré with no single contralateral forward arm vs a more open lyrical continuation of the II opposition line that preserves the front-arm-opposite relationship.
* Whether Arabesque IV is the inclined opposition form of II or a closed/same-side/high-fifth finish.

Current working interpretation remains the textbook Vaganova mapping with I = arms in seconde, II = upright contralateral opposition, III = closed lyrical, IV = inclined contralateral opposition, i.e. the front arm opposite the lifted leg is taught in Arabesques II and IV, E second and fourth. This fits the classic description of the Vaganova diagonal made long by carrying the forward arm on the side of the supporting leg opposite the lifted leg.

B second and third is the strongest alternative, reflecting syllabus variants that describe III as a continuation of the II opposition line with the contralateral front arm preserved and IV as closed. C first and third reflects an alternative numbering convention / French-style offset where the opposition pair is I/III.

No firm consensus yet; canonical Vaganova source verification on the definition of III and IV is still needed before finalising.
