Leg remains derrière, torso a little more ouvert / cambré, arm line worked higher / rounder / more lyrical, but port de bras remains contralateral: the forward-projected arm is still the supporting-side arm extended in front on the side opposite the lifted leg with the back arm on the line of the lifted leg. The clear single-arm forward-opposite diagonal of II is lost; carriage becomes contained / same-side / gathered.

The deliberation has now converged unanimously in round 3 on B. Second and third.

Common agreed anatomy of the Vaganova derrière series:
* The four numbers are a port de bras / épaulement series with the working leg held en arabesque derrière.
* Arabesque I is the en face / symmetrical base in the current syllabus. Arms are taught essentially in open seconde / high first to the sides, both on one level, torso upright/en face. No single isolated arm is clearly projected en avant in opposition to the working leg. This disqualifies any answer containing I.
* Arabesque II is the classic épaulement croisé / opposition. Working leg derrière, torso in profile/effacé. The arm on the supporting/standing side is carried en avant in front of the torso and the arm on the working-leg side is carried en arrière on the line of the leg. Right leg back = left arm forward. The forward arm is contralateral, i.e. extended in front on the side opposite the lifted leg. This is unambiguous.
* Arabesque III is the lyrical continuation / opening / cambré development of II. Leg remains derrière, torso a little more ouvert/cambré, arm line worked higher/rounder/more lyrical, but the port de bras remains contralateral: the forward-projected arm is still the supporting-side arm extended in front on the side opposite the lifted leg, with the back arm on the line of the lifted leg. II and III are taught as the upright opposition and its open/lyrical continuation.
* Arabesque IV closes the line. Arms are brought together/gathered toward a high fifth/rounded fifth/crossed first carriage in front of the chest, torso inclines forward. The clear single-arm forward-opposite diagonal of II is lost; the carriage becomes contained/same-side.

Why earlier alternatives were rejected:
* First and third camp relied on an alternative odd=opposition numbering convention where I and III are the en ligne/croisé arabesques with forward arm opposite leg and II/IV are same-side. Under the current Vaganova syllabus numbering used by the majority, I has no forward arm and II is the opposition.
* Second and fourth minority treated III as closed/both-arms-in-front/lyrical with no single contrasted forward arm and IV as the inclined opposition. Round 3 consensus treats III as the open opposition continuation and IV as the closed finish.

Evidence consistently cited: Vaganova manuals describe II as upright épaulement croisé, III as the cambré opening of the same croisé line, I as arms-in-seconde base, IV as the gathered/high-fifth finish.

Unresolved nuance still noted by some colleagues: school-to-school sourcebook variation in naming III vs IV exists historically, but under the standard numbering used in the current deliberation the “single arm extended in front on the side opposite the lifted leg” criterion is satisfied by the open opposition pair II and III.

My current best answer is B. Second and third.

B. Second and third

The derrière series in Vaganova is a port de bras / épaulement series with the working leg held en arabesque derrière. The criterion in the question is the classic Vaganova épaulement croisé / opposition line: a single arm carried en avant on the supporting / standing side, i.e. contralateral to the lifted leg, with the other arm carried en arrière on the line of the lifted leg.

* Arabesque I is the syllabus en face / symmetrical base. Arms are taught essentially in an open seconde / high first to the sides of the torso, en face and upright. There is no single isolated arm projected en avant in opposition to the working leg.

* Arabesque II is the textbook opposition / croisé. Working leg derrière, torso in profile / effacé. The supporting-side arm is taken en avant in front of the torso and the working-leg-side arm is taken en arrière on the line of the leg. Right leg back = left arm forward, right arm back. The forward arm is contralateral, extended in front on the side opposite the lifted leg.

* Arabesque III is the lyrical continuation / opening / cambré development of II. Leg remains derrière, torso a little more ouvert / cambré and the arm line is worked higher and more rounded, but the port de bras remains contralateral: the forward-projected arm is still the supporting-side arm, extended in front on the side opposite the lifted leg, with the back arm on the line of the lifted leg. II and III are taught as the upright and open / lyrical opposition pair.

* Arabesque IV closes the line. Arms are brought together toward a high fifth / rounded fifth / gathered cambré carriage in front of the chest and the torso inclines forward. The clear single-arm forward-opposite diagonal of II is lost; the carriage becomes contained / same-side.

The two Vaganova derrière arabesques consistently taught with a single arm extended in front on the supporting side, i.e. on the side opposite the raised leg, are the open opposition arabesques II and III.

reflection_text.1:
The anatomical fact remains settled and now unanimous across round 4: the Vaganova derrière series is a port de bras / épaulement series with working leg en arrière. The question criterion is the classic épaulement croisé / opposition diagonal: a single arm carried en avant on the supporting/standing side, i.e. contralateral to the lifted leg, with the other arm en arrière on the line of the lifted leg.

Consensus mapping stable from Round-3 and reinforced in Round-4:
* Arabesque I = en face / symmetrical base in the English Vaganova syllabus. Arms essentially in open seconde / high first to the sides, torso upright/en face. No single isolated arm projected en avant in opposition; line is symmetrical, no forward-opposite diagonal.
* Arabesque II = classic profile opposition / croisé. Working leg derrière, torso profile/effacé. Supporting-side arm en avant in front of torso, working-leg-side arm en arrière on line of leg. Right leg back = left arm forward. Forward arm is contralateral, opposite lifted leg.
* Arabesque III = lyrical continuation / opening / cambré development of II. Leg remains derrière, torso slightly more ouvert/cambré, arms worked higher/rounder/more lyrical, but port de bras remains contralateral: forward-projected arm is still supporting-side arm extended in front on side opposite lifted leg, back arm on line of leg. II and III are the open opposition pair, upright and open/lyrical.
* Arabesque IV = closed finish. Arms brought together toward high fifth/rounded fifth/gathered/crossed first in front of chest, torso inclined forward. Clear single-arm forward-opposite diagonal of II is lost; carriage becomes contained/same-side.

Hence the two arabesques consistently taught with a single arm extended in front on the supporting side, i.e. on the side opposite the raised leg, are Arabesque II and Arabesque III. That is option B. Second and third.

Meta-note retained: older Russian pedagogical texts number the opposition family 1/3 and same-side family 2/4. The anatomy is the same; under the English Vaganova syllabus numbering now adopted by the whole group, the opposition is numbered II and III. Round 0 showed wide spread: E, C, B, D etc. After deliberation, all 21 colleagues in Round 4 now give B, with no dissent remaining. No unresolved questions remain on the mapping under the chosen numbering convention.
